questions.q: State the primary theme of the chapter "vlxj otkgr" in one sentence.
questions.a: The primary theme is the abuse of power and the systemic exploitation of the weak by the strong across different social hierarchies. A wrong answer like "The stories are about animals and kings" reveals the student is confusing subject matter with theme; they have identified topics but not the underlying idea the author explores.

questions.q: Explain in your own words how the story 'ksj illustrates the primary theme of the chapter.
questions.a: In 'ksj, the protagonist 'ksj is a helpless being whose very existence is ignored by the passing travelers until the narrator's intervention; this mirrors how the powerful (travelers/king) remain indifferent to the suffering of the powerless until forced to acknowledge it. A wrong answer that only summarizes the plot ("A man sees a bird and saves it") shows the student cannot move from literal events to thematic significance.

questions.q: Using the story igpku, identify two specific actions the king takes that demonstrate the theme of "power corrupting accountability" and explain the consequence of each action on the subjects.
questions.a: Action 1: The king orders everyone to cover their eyes so they cannot see his misrule — consequence: subjects lose the ability to witness injustice and thus cannot resist. Action 2: The king orders them to plug their ears so they cannot hear cries of distress — consequence: communication breaks down, isolating individuals and preventing collective action. A wrong answer listing actions without linking consequences to the theme shows application without analysis.

questions.q: Compare the portrayal of the exploiter in pkj gkFk (the landlord) and lk>k (the horse-master). What common trait do they share, and how does the author use their different settings to universalize the theme?
questions.a: Both exploiters prioritize profit over the lives of those they control: the landlord calculates labor output in "four legs" and discards workers when they become unproductive; the horse-master forces the horse to race until death for prize money. The rural village and the racetrack settings show exploitation is not confined to one sphere — it operates in agriculture, industry, and entertainment alike. A wrong answer that treats the two exploiters as completely different "because one is a farmer and one is a trainer" misses the author's deliberate cross-setting parallelism.

questions.q: Evaluate whether the endings of the four stories collectively support a message of hope or despair. Justify with evidence from at least two stories.
questions.a: The endings lean toward cautious hope: in 'ksj the narrator's intervention saves the bird, suggesting individual conscience can disrupt indifference; in lk>k the horse's death exposes the master's cruelty, implying truth eventually surfaces. However, igpku ends with the king still ruling, and pkj gkFk ends with the landlord unpunished, so hope is not guaranteed — it requires sustained resistance. A wrong answer saying "All endings are sad" ignores the subtle agency shown by the narrator in 'ksj and the implicit critique in lk>k, revealing a binary (hope/despair) reading instead of nuanced evaluation.

questions.q: Write a 50-word micro-story that captures the primary theme of this chapter in a contemporary Indian setting (e.g., a gig worker, a migrant laborer, a student).
questions.a: A delivery partner cycles through monsoon floods, app tracking his every pause; the algorithm docks pay for "late" orders caused by flooded roads. He sees his manager's bonus notification pop up on the same screen. He stops, types "We are not machines" in the chat group — fifty others reply within minutes. A poor answer would be a generic sad story without the specific power dynamic (algorithm vs worker) and the spark of collective voice, showing inability to transfer the theme to a new context.
